A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaRFT work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original training experiments, benchmark accuracies, efficiency measurements, difficulty-estimation analyses, and experiments with extreme difficulty distributions.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, target-reward ablations, alternative RL algorithms, and experiments using LLM-estimated difficulty.

M1.justification: The nearest-difficulty sampler, binary reward, and clipped tanh update remain unchanged. V3 adds an evaluated difficulty-scoring variant using GPT-4o judgments clipped to a 1–5 scale, with the update step size rescaled to 2.5 (Appendices A.5 and B.3).

E1.justification: Both versions use DeepScaleR and the same six evaluation benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH 500, OlympiadBench, Minerva Math, AMC 23, and AIME 24. The three main difficulty distributions and two extreme distributions are retained; the extreme-distribution study moves from Section 6.2 to Appendix A.3. Added experiments use the existing data and tasks.

E2.justification: V3 adds PPO with filtered data and PPO with a fixed curriculum to the main comparisons in Figure 3 and Tables 1–2. Appendix A.4 also evaluates GRPO and REINFORCE++ against their AdaRFT variants; these algorithms were only discussed as compatible options in v1.

E3.justification: The 7B efficiency comparison changes its AdaRFT reference checkpoint from step 60 to step 40, and reported smoothing changes from 0.7 to 0.3. New protocols include pass@40 filtering at the 10% and 90% thresholds, a linear fixed curriculum, and target-reward sweeps. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds training-dynamics analysis against a fixed curriculum, an ablation comparing target rewards 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8, and analyses of optimizer compatibility and rollout-based versus GPT-4o difficulty scoring (Appendices A.1, A.2, A.4, and A.5). The earlier subsampling and extreme-difficulty analyses remain.

E5.justification: V3 introduces Pearson correlation significance reporting, with p < 0.05 for both difficulty-label comparisons. Figure 3 adds raw-accuracy bands of ±1 percentage point, explicitly described as visual guides rather than confidence intervals. The ten subsampling trials remain unchanged, and neither version reports training seeds or repeated-training uncertainty.

E6.justification: The original step-100 PPO and AdaRFT accuracy entries in Table 2 are retained, while substantial baseline and ablation results are added. Efficiency values change: for 1.5B skew-difficult training, PPO's reported extra steps change from 26 (43.67%) to 43 (71.7%) under the revised analysis protocol. V1's step-60 per-benchmark accuracy breakdown is removed.

T1.justification: New Section 3.4 introduces entropy-regularized policy and value definitions and a claimed KL–reward-variance bound to justify a target reward of 0.5. Appendix B.2 adds a linear-mapping derivation of the existing update. These are substantive mathematical additions, although Equations 1–3 contain inconsistent normalization.

C1.justification: The abstract changes the headline efficiency claim from up to 2× fewer training steps to up to 2× lower training time. The central claims of adaptive difficulty selection, improved efficiency and accuracy, and unchanged reward functions and model architecture remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations of fixed-curriculum failure, target-reward sensitivity, and the usefulness of approximate LLM difficulty judgments. Its limitations discussion newly defends fixed offline scores as solver-independent and claims functional equivalence to online difficulty estimation. V1's future-work proposals involving richer training signals and co-adapting the optimizer are dropped.

D1.justification: Appendix B and Table 3 expand configuration documentation to PPO, GRPO, and REINFORCE++, while Tables 4–7 supply the GPT-4o scoring prompt, rubric, and examples. The executable PPO configuration from v1 is replaced by a parameter table, losing some padding, offloading, and checkpoint details. The advertised code address also changes.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning against staged curricula, online difficulty filtering, and fixed schedules, adding works by Wen, Song, Bae, and Parashar, among others. It also introduces literature supporting the new theoretical argument. V1 primarily positioned AdaRFT against algorithmic simplification and static data selection.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are substantially rewritten and condensed. Results and discussion are reorganized into Results and Analysis, Limitations, and an expanded discussion appendix. Implementation material moves to Appendix B, and Appendix C adds a writing-assistance disclosure.

P2.justification: The paper switches from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 gains an LLM-difficulty panel, Figure 3 gains comparison curves and shading, Table 1 is redesigned, and Table 2 moves to the appendix with additional rows. New analysis plots and configuration/prompt tables substantially expand the displays; v1's Figure 4 is retained as v3's Figure 6.

improvement.justification: Curriculum-specific controls and direct tests of target reward, optimizer compatibility, and cheaper difficulty scoring strengthen v1's empirical case. Expanded configuration and prompts also help reproduction. However, new Section 3.4 introduces normalization inconsistencies, and Equation 4 fails at p = 0.5, tau = 1: Equations 2–3 give KL approximately 0.1201, below the claimed 0.125 bound. These correctness problems temper the overall gain.
